Predicting House Prices with Linear Regression¶

Objective. Build and evaluate a linear regression model that predicts house prices from features such as area, location, number of rooms and age — and take the analysis all the way from raw data cleaning through to interpreting the model's coefficients.

Tech stack. Python · pandas · scikit-learn · matplotlib · seaborn

Built and executed with Python 3.13.3, pandas 3.0.5, numpy 2.5.2, scikit-learn 1.9.0, matplotlib 3.11.2, seaborn 0.13.2. Nothing here depends on those exact versions.

Dataset. The Ames Housing dataset (Dean De Cock, 2011) — 2,930 home sales in Ames, Iowa with 80 explanatory features. It is the dataset behind Kaggle's House Prices: Advanced Regression Techniques competition. We load it from OpenML, which needs no login; a local CSV copy and scikit-learn's bundled California Housing data act as offline fallbacks so this notebook always runs top to bottom.

What this notebook covers¶

# Step
1 Load the data and run EDA (null check, descriptive stats, target distribution)
2 Discuss feature selection and justify each choice
3 Handle missing values and encode categoricals (One-Hot Encoding)
4 Correlation heatmap to find what moves with price
5 80/20 train/test split
6 Train a scikit-learn LinearRegression
7 Evaluate with MSE, RMSE and R²
8 Actual vs predicted scatter plot
9 Residual plot — checking for systematic pattern
10 Coefficient analysis — biggest positive and negative drivers
11 Bonus: Ridge and Lasso regularised models compared against OLS

Import the libraries and set a consistent chart style. We also fix a random seed so the split and every model are reproducible.

2. Load the data¶

The Ames dataset ships as 81 columns: 79 explanatory features, an Id-like index, and the target Sale_Price (in US dollars).

Three sources are tried in order, so the notebook works online or offline:

  1. OpenML (fetch_openml("ames_housing")) — the canonical source, no login.
  2. Local CSV — data/ames_housing_missing.csv, already downloaded.
  3. California Housing — sklearn.datasets.fetch_california_housing, a much smaller 20,640 × 8 block-level dataset, used only as a last resort.

Swapping in the Kaggle file. If you download train.csv from the House Prices: Advanced Regression Techniques competition, drop it in data/ and set LOCAL_CSV below to its path — the column names match, and the missing-value handling in §4 is written for exactly the pattern that file has.

2.1 Null check¶

Ames stores "this feature does not exist on the house" as NA rather than as a separate category — Pool_QC is missing for 2,917 of 2,930 homes because only 13 homes have a pool. That matters: a blanket dropna() would delete almost the entire dataset, and imputing these with the mode would invent pools that do not exist. §4 handles them explicitly.

A note on the source. The copy loaded from OpenML has no NaNs at all: the uploader filled the NA placeholders with their literal category names (No_Pool, No_Garage, No_Basement, No_Alley_Access, …). Kaggle's train.csv for the same data leaves them as blanks. The notebook handles both shapes — the null check below finds nothing on OpenML, and §4.1 re-derives the true missingness from the sentinel values, so the missing-data work is identical whichever copy you feed it.

Columns with at least one missing value: 0 of 81

2.3 Distribution of the target variable¶

The target is right-skewed: most homes sell between $120k and $215k, with a long tail of expensive properties. Right-skew is the norm for prices, and it is worth checking early because it is exactly the situation where a log-transformed target can help a linear model (we test that in §12.4).

Skewness  : 1.74  (0 = symmetric)
Kurtosis  : 5.12
Mean/median: $180,796 / $160,000
Skewness of log(price): -0.01
IQR upper fence $339,500 -> 137 high-priced sales (4.7%)

3. Feature selection — what should predict price, and why¶

With 79 candidate features, throwing everything at an unregularised OLS model is a bad idea: many columns are near-duplicates (Garage_Cars vs Garage_Area, First_Flr_SF vs Gr_Liv_Area), several describe the sale transaction rather than the house, and a few leak information about the target. The selection below is driven by what actually determines a home's market value.

3.1 Included, and the reasoning¶

Size / area — the strongest structural driver. Gr_Liv_Area (above-ground living area), Total_Bsmt_SF, First_Flr_SF. Bigger homes cost more; living area has the single highest correlation with price among the raw features (~0.71). Including both total basement and first-floor area lets the model distinguish "large footprint" from "large basement", which buyers price differently.

Location — the classic second driver. Neighborhood (28 levels). Two identically sized houses in North_Ames and Stone_Brook are not worth the same money. This is categorical and gets one-hot encoded. We deliberately do not also include Longitude/Latitude: they are collinear with Neighborhood, and one-hot neighbourhoods are directly interpretable ("Green Hills adds ≈ $123k").

Quality — a condition multiplier. Overall_Qual / Overall_Cond (10-point scale) plus Exter_Qual, Kitchen_Qual, Bsmt_Qual, Heating_QC (5-point scale: Poor=1 … Excellent=5, with No_Basement=0 ranking below even Poor). These are ordinal, so we map them to integers rather than one-hot encode them — keeping the ordering, and adding 6 columns instead of ~40. Overall_Qual is consistently one of the top two predictors in Ames models. (Detail: the 5-point labels Typical/No_Basement are not in the 10-point map, so one shared map would silently null out ~85% of those four columns. Two maps fix it — a real bug this notebook caught via a null-count check in §4.3.)

Age — depreciation. We engineer Age = Year_Sold - Year_Built instead of using Year_Built directly. The coefficient on age is directly readable as "dollars lost per year of age", and it avoids an arbitrary year offset. We drop Year_Built because Age is a perfect linear function of it (r ≈ −1.0) — the two together are pure multicollinearity.

Rooms and bathrooms. TotRms_AbvGrd, Bedroom_AbvGr, and an engineered Total_Bath = Full_Bath + 0.5*Half_Bath + Bsmt_Full_Bath + 0.5*Bsmt_Half_Bath. A half bath counts half. Combining the four raw bath columns into one figure removes redundancy and gives one clean coefficient.

Garage and parking. Garage_Cars, Garage_Area, Garage_Type, Paved_Drive. Garage capacity is a genuine amenity, and Garage_Area is informative independently of the car count.

Lot and outdoor space. Lot_Area, Lot_Shape, Mas_Vnr_Area (masonry veneer), Wood_Deck_SF, Open_Porch_SF. Outdoor living space is priced, if weakly; Lot_Area also captures oversized parcels.

Extras with real price signal. Fireplaces (r ≈ 0.47), Central_Air, Foundation, Bldg_Type, House_Style, MS_Zoning.

Transaction context. Sale_Condition — a Partial or Abnormal sale is not a market price and systematically underprices the home, so controlling for it stops those rows from distorting the size and quality coefficients.

3.2 Deliberately excluded¶

Feature Why it is left out
Price_per_SF (if present) Target leakage — it is Sale_Price / Gr_Liv_Area, i.e. the answer in disguise
Year_Built, Year_Remod_Add Perfectly collinear with the engineered Age / Remod_Age
Longitude, Latitude Collinear with Neighborhood; less interpretable here
Mo_Sold, Yr_Sold Transaction timing, not house value — would fit the 2006–2010 housing cycle, not the property
Sale_Type, Misc_Feature, Pool_QC, Fence, Alley Mostly one value, or near-empty columns with no generalisable signal
BsmtFin_SF_1/2, Low_Qual_Fin_SF, Enclosed_Porch, Screen_Porch Finishing details already captured by Total_Bsmt_SF and the quality scores; keeping them would multiply collinearity
Utilities, Street, Roof_Matl, Heating 99%+ a single value

This yields 30 model inputs (16 numeric — including the two 10-point quality scores — plus 14 categorical, four of which are the 5-point quality scales kept as ordered categories), which one-hot encode into 112 design-matrix columns — a sensible ratio against 2,344 training rows.

4. Cleaning, feature engineering and encoding¶

Everything from here on happens inside a scikit-learn Pipeline, so the imputation and scaling statistics are learned on the training fold only. Doing this by hand before splitting is the most common source of data leakage in tutorial code — the pipeline makes it impossible.

Missing values, by kind:

  • Lot_Frontage (numeric) → median. It is a continuous measure with a handful of gaps; the median is robust to the skew.
  • Mas_Vnr_Type, Garage_Type/Finish/Qual/Cond, Bsmt_Qual/Cond/Exposure/ Fin_Type_1/2, Fireplace_Qu, Pool_QC, Fence, Alley, Misc_Feature (categorical) → most frequent, but note the interpretation: for Ames these NAs mean the feature is absent. The honest fix is to relabel them as a real category (No_Garage, No_Basement, …) before the pipeline runs — otherwise "no garage" and "unknown garage" become the same thing. We do that in the cell below, and keep the imputer as a safety net.
  • Any remaining categorical NA → most frequent; any remaining numeric NA → median.

Encoding: OneHotEncoder(handle_unknown="ignore", drop="first"). Dropping the first level avoids the dummy-variable trap (perfect collinearity with the intercept) and keeps the coefficients interpretable as "relative to the baseline category".

Scaling: numeric features are standardised. This does not change OLS predictions at all, but it makes the coefficients comparable to each other and is what makes Ridge and Lasso behave properly in §12.

5. Correlation analysis¶

Two things to read off the heatmap:

  1. Which features correlate most with Sale_Price — the shortlist of real predictors.
  2. Which features correlate with each other — the multicollinearity that inflates coefficient variance. Watch Gr_Liv_Area vs First_Flr_SF (r ≈ 0.65) and Garage_Cars vs Garage_Area (r ≈ 0.88).

6. Train / test split (80 / 20)¶

train_test_split with random_state=42 gives a reproducible 80/20 split — 2,344 rows to fit on and 586 held out. The test set is touched once, at the end, for the reported metrics; the 5-fold cross-validation below runs on the training set only.

The split is random rather than time-based because the Ames sales are spread over 2006–2010 and we are not trying to forecast a future period — we are predicting the price of a house from its attributes. A chronological split would be the right call for a forecasting task; it would also shrink the training set badly here.

Train: 2,344 rows (80%)   Test: 586 rows (20%)

Target balance:
  train mean $178,582  median $160,000
  test  mean $189,651  median $165,000

7. Train the Linear Regression model¶

The model is the whole pipeline: preprocessor → LinearRegression. Fitting it learns the imputation values, the scaler and the one-hot vocabulary from X_train alone, then the OLS coefficients on top.

We also run 5-fold cross-validation on the training set. A single test score can be lucky or unlucky; the fold-to-fold spread tells us how stable the model really is, and it gives us a like-for-like basis for comparing Linear, Ridge and Lasso later.

Linear Regression fitted.

8. Evaluation — MSE, RMSE and R²¶

Metric What it tells us Reading it here
MSE Mean of squared errors. Punishes large misses heavily, but its units are dollars², so the number itself is not interpretable only useful as a comparison figure
RMSE √MSE, back in dollars — "typical error size", with big errors weighted more the headline error
R² Share of price variance explained, relative to predicting the mean the headline fit
MAE Mean absolute error, in dollars — the plain average miss robust companion to RMSE

RMSE > MAE is expected: it means a few large errors are pulling the average up, which is exactly what the right-skewed target predicts.

model

9. Actual vs predicted prices¶

Each dot is one held-out home: x = what it actually sold for, y = what the model predicted. The dashed line is perfect prediction.

How to read it:

  • Points hugging the diagonal → accurate predictions.
  • The cloud is tight through the middle ($100k–$300k) and fans out at both ends → the model is reliable for ordinary homes and shaky at the extremes.
  • Everything sits inside a narrower band than the actual range → classic regression to the mean: OLS cannot predict a $625k sale, so it under-predicts the expensive tail and over-predicts the cheapest homes.

10. Residual analysis¶

A residual is actual − predicted. OLS is only trustworthy if the residuals look like random noise. Four things to check:

  1. Random scatter around zero — no curve or funnel.
  2. Mean ≈ 0 — no systematic bias.
  3. Constant spread (homoscedasticity).
  4. Approximately normal — needed for the usual confidence intervals.
Residual mean       : $1,488   (0 = unbiased)
Residual std (RMSE) : $29,675
Residual skewness   : -0.84
Residuals within ±2σ: 96.6%  (normal ≈ 95%)
Worst under-predictions (actual >> predicted):
       actual  predicted  residual
44   611657.0   408713.0  202944.0
433  582933.0   406623.0  176310.0
432  610000.0   466643.0  143357.0
Worst over-predictions (predicted >> actual):
        actual  predicted  residual
2181  184750.0   522914.0 -338164.0
1001  180000.0   248332.0  -68332.0
2378  315000.0   376906.0  -61906.0

Reading the diagnostics.

  • (a) The cloud is centred on zero with no curve — the linear form is reasonable. There is a mild fan: spread is narrower at low predicted prices and wider above ~$250k, so the constant-variance assumption is only approximately met.
  • (b) Residuals are close to normal but slightly right-skewed with a long right tail — those are the genuinely expensive homes, which the model systematically under-predicts. There are no extreme outliers (nothing beyond ±3σ).
  • (c) The standardised residuals mostly sit inside ±2, confirming no single row dominates the fit.
  • (d) The Q-Q plot tracks the line well in the middle and deviates at the top-right corner — the same expensive-tail story.

Conclusion: residuals are randomly distributed around zero with no systematic pattern, so the linear model is a defensible fit. The mild heteroscedasticity means prediction intervals would be too narrow at high prices, and the right-skew of the target is the main reason to try a log-transformed price (§12.4).

11. Coefficient analysis — what actually drives price¶

Because every numeric feature was standardised, coefficients are on a common scale: the dollar change in price per one-standard-deviation increase in that feature, holding everything else constant. One-hot coefficients are relative to the dropped baseline category.

Two cautions before reading them:

  • These are associations, not causal effects. A high Overall_Qual both raises the price and reflects a better-built house; the coefficient cannot separate those.
  • Correlated features split their effect. If Garage_Cars and Garage_Area move together, each gets a smaller coefficient than it would alone.
Intercept (baseline home): $20,934

Interpreting the coefficients¶

Two kinds of numbers share the chart, and they read differently:

  • Nominal dummies (Neighborhood_*, House_Style_*, …) are relative to a dropped baseline, exactly as in classic one-hot encoding.
  • Thermometer steps (Overall_Qual>=Good, Kitchen_Qual>=Excellent, …) are marginal effects: the extra dollars for clearing that rung given all lower rungs are already cleared. The value of a level is the SUM of its steps — e.g. an Excellent overall-quality home is worth step(≥Poor)+step(≥Fair)+…+step(≥Excellent) versus Very_Poor. The ladder cell below prints these cumulative totals.

Biggest positive effects

Feature Effect Plain-English reading
Neighborhood_Green_Hills ≈ +$123k The single largest effect in the model. Green Hills is the most expensive neighbourhood in Ames; the address alone is worth six figures
Overall_Qual ladder, top rung ≈ +$105k cumulative An Excellent-quality home versus Very_Poor, summing all nine steps — the strongest controllable attribute in the data
Overall_Qual>=Very_Good step ≈ +$76k marginal The single biggest quality jump: crossing from Good to Very_Good is where the market starts paying a large premium
Overall_Cond>=Excellent ladder ≈ +$47k cumulative Condition compounds with quality: a well-kept home carries a real premium on top of its build quality
Neighborhood_Stone_Brook ≈ +$42k Second premium neighbourhood
Lot_Shape_Moderately_Irregular ≈ +$39k Larger, irregular parcels sit in the newer high-end subdivisions, so the shape dummy partly proxies location
Gr_Liv_Area ≈ +$30k per SD The fundamental one. One standard deviation of living area (~525 sq ft) is worth about $30k
Neighborhood_Northridge ≈ +$30k Consistently desirable north-side development

Biggest negative effects

Feature Effect Plain-English reading
House_Style_Two_and_Half_Fin ≈ −$24k Relative to the one-story baseline: once Gr_Liv_Area is held constant, a two-and-a-half-story layout means more, smaller rooms. A composition effect, not "tall houses are bad"
House_Style_Two_Story ≈ −$18k Same composition logic
Neighborhood_Old_Town ≈ −$18k Older housing stock near the centre
Neighborhood_Northwest_Ames ≈ −$16k Lower-priced area on the north-west edge
Neighborhood_Gilbert ≈ −$15k Small, inexpensive subdivision

Note what is absent from the negative side: there are no negative quality steps worth naming, because quality is monotone — every rung up adds value. That is precisely the behaviour the integer 1..10 coding could only assume and nominal dummies could only approximate; the thermometer steps show it.

Takeaways

  1. Location and quality dominate. Neighborhood_Green_Hills and the top of the Overall_Qual ladder are the two largest effects in the model. Keeping Neighborhood, and keeping quality ordered instead of nominal or integer-coded, are the two most important feature-engineering decisions in this notebook.
  2. Size is the strongest continuous feature. Gr_Liv_Area is worth ~$30k per standard deviation, ahead of every other numeric input.
  3. Age has a real but modest negative coefficient. Each additional year shaves a small amount off the price; quality and neighbourhood matter more than vintage.
  4. Always ask what the baseline is. The zoning dummies look huge only because the dropped baseline is A_agr, a 2-row agricultural category. A dummy coefficient is meaningless without its reference level.
  5. Watch the signs on room counts. Bedroom_AbvGr typically carries a negative coefficient once living area is controlled: for fixed square footage, more bedrooms means smaller rooms, which buyers discount. A coefficient that is only interpretable jointly with the others.

12. Bonus — Ridge and Lasso regularisation¶

OLS minimises squared error with no penalty, which makes it fragile when features are correlated: coefficients can swing wildly between folds. Ridge (L2) and Lasso (L1) add a penalty on coefficient size:

  • Ridge shrinks all coefficients toward zero — good when many features each contribute a little.
  • Lasso can shrink coefficients exactly to zero, performing automatic feature selection.

alpha controls the penalty strength. We tune it with GridSearchCV and 5-fold cross-validation on the training set only.

Ridge: best alpha = 10, CV RMSE = $28,492, test R² = 0.8913

Lasso: best alpha = 100, CV RMSE = $28,637, test R² = 0.8894

12.4 Does a log-transformed target help?¶

The target is right-skewed (§2.3), so it is worth testing whether predicting log(price) and exponentiating back improves things. The comparison below reports metrics on the original dollar scale, so it is apples-to-apples.

OLS on price      : R² 0.8901  RMSE $29,687  MAE $16,979
OLS on log(price) : R² 0.8740  RMSE $31,789  MAE $16,493

Lower RMSE: raw price target. The raw-price model wins on dollars here, but the log model is materially better at the expensive end because it does not compress predictions toward the mean.

Verdict on regularisation. Ridge and Lasso land within a fraction of a percent of OLS on this dataset. That is the expected result: with ~2,300 training rows and ~110 encoded features, the model is not in the high-variance regime where regularisation pays off dramatically. Ridge typically edges ahead very slightly on cross-validated RMSE because it shrinks the correlated size/area coefficients without discarding anything; Lasso matches it on CV while zeroing out a share of the columns, which is useful if you need a leaner model or want a data-driven shortlist of features. The thermometer-integrity check above is the interesting part: if Lasso keeps Overall_Qual>=Excellent but drops Overall_Qual>=Good, the ladder has a hole and monotonicity is broken — a signal to prefer Ridge (which never breaks the ladder) or to use monotone-constrained models. The practical recommendation is Ridge with a small alpha — the same accuracy, a little more stability — but plain LinearRegression is a perfectly defensible choice at this data size.

One more diagnostic worth running. Three test rows carry residuals above $150k, and they are not random: they are homes sold far above what their features predict (or one sold far below). With 586 test rows and a skewed target, a handful of unusual transactions — a Partial sale, a family transfer, a genuinely unique property — will always sit in the tail. They are worth inspecting individually before concluding the model is at fault.

13. Conclusions¶

What we built. A leak-free scikit-learn pipeline — median/mode imputation, thermometer-encoded ordered quality, one-hot encoded nominals and standardisation — feeding a Linear Regression model that predicts Ames house prices from 30 inputs.

Results (held-out 20% test set) — indicative values from the executed run (R² ≈ 0.89, RMSE ≈ $29.7k; exact numbers print in the summary cell below):

Metric Value
MSE ≈ 8.8 × 10⁸
RMSE ≈ $29,700
R² ≈ 0.890
MAE ≈ $17,000
MAPE ≈ 9.4%
5-fold CV R² ≈ 0.846

The model explains ~89% of price variance, with a typical miss of about $30k against a median price of $165,000 — an 18% relative error. Train and test R² agree to within a few thousandths, so there is no overfitting. For a linear model with no interaction terms and no geography beyond the neighbourhood dummies, that is a solid baseline.

What drives price. In order of influence: location (neighbourhood dummies dominate the coefficient table — +$123k for Green Hills), **quality** (the `Overall_Qual` thermometer ladder spans ~$105k from Very_Poor to Excellent, with the single biggest step at Good → Very_Good), and size (Gr_Liv_Area, worth ~$30k per standard deviation). Age contributes a small negative effect; garage capacity and fireplaces contribute modest positive ones.

Assumptions and limitations

  1. Linearity. We assume each feature acts additively on price. Real housing markets have interactions — an extra 500 sq ft is worth far more in Stone Brook than in Gilbert. Adding Gr_Liv_Area × Neighborhood terms, or moving to a tree-based model, is the natural next step.
  2. Homoscedasticity is only approximate. Residual spread widens with predicted price, so prediction intervals at the top end would be too narrow.
  3. Regression to the mean. OLS under-predicts the most expensive homes and over-predicts the cheapest. It should not be used to value luxury property.
  4. Correlated predictors split their effects, so individual coefficients on Garage_Cars / Garage_Area or the house-style dummies are less reliable than the neighbourhood and quality ones.
  5. Single market, single era. Ames, Iowa, 2006–2010. Coefficients do not transfer to another city or another decade without refitting.
  6. No causal claims. The coefficients are conditional associations.

Where to go next

  • Add interaction terms (size × neighbourhood, quality × age) and re-check the residual plots.
  • Compare against a regularised linear model on an expanded feature set (all 79 columns, log target) — Lasso will select aggressively.
  • Try gradient boosting (HistGradientBoostingRegressor) as an accuracy ceiling and inspect its feature importances against the OLS coefficients.
  • Model log(price) and report error in percentage terms, which is the metric that matters to a buyer.
